title: P-values, Hypothesis Tests & Better Empirical Practice
excerpt: Test a specific claim against a stated model and learn what a p-value measures: how surprising the data would be if that model were true. Put it alongside effect size, uncertainty and study design; a value below 0.05 is not proof, practical importance or the chance that a claim is false.
objectives: State null and alternative hypotheses and identify one- or two-sided tests.
Interpret a p-value conditionally on a null model, study design and analysis assumptions.
Calculate a simple test statistic and connect p-values with effect sizes and interval estimates.
Explain Type I error, Type II error, power, multiplicity and the role of preregistration.
Separate association, prediction, causality, uncertainty and practical or economic importance.

lessons.title: Start with a question, design and null model
lessons.body:
A test should follow a question, not replace one. Define the estimand, unit, population, outcome, time window and comparison. The null hypothesis H₀ is a precise reference claim, such as a mean abnormal return μ equal to 0 percentage points; the alternative H₁ describes a departure, such as μ not equal to 0 for a two-sided test. A design determines what observations can be compared, while assumptions describe how the test statistic behaves if H₀ is true. Random assignment can support causal interpretation; an observational event study usually describes an association unless stronger identification assumptions hold. A p-value is evidence about compatibility with this specified model, not a verdict about reality.

Begin by writing the comparison in the units that a reader can audit. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose the estimand is the difference in mean monthly spending between two customer groups, measured in US dollars per customer during January 2026. If group A averages $42 and group B $39, the estimated difference is $42 − $39 = $3 per customer per month. A null of zero says the population difference is $0 per customer per month for the defined groups and period; it does not say every customer spends equally. A survey sample may support an association, but it does not by itself show that membership caused spending. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST — Use and Interpretation of P-Values’ in the linked sources.

A useful design can make the null reflect a decision threshold rather than merely zero. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a retailer pre-specifies the estimand as the population change in fulfillment cost per order, in US dollars per order, after a routing rule; negative values mean savings. If the minimum worthwhile saving is $0.50, a one-sided test can set H₀: μ = −$0.50 (or, for a conservative decision rule, μ ≥ −$0.50) against H₁: μ < −$0.50. Imagine the sample estimate is −$0.80 per order with standard error $0.20 per order. The standardized distance from the boundary is t = [−0.80 − (−0.50)]/$0.20 = −$0.30/$0.20 = −1.5, so a normal one-sided approximation gives p ≈ 0.067. At α = 0.05, this is insufficient evidence that savings reach the $0.50 threshold; it does not prove that savings are absent. The calculation also assumes independent observations and a suitable standard-error model; repeated orders from the same customer or warehouse would require dependence-aware uncertainty, and the routing rule’s observational comparison would still not establish causality without a credible design.
lessons.takeaway: A p-value inherits the question, design, null model and assumptions used to produce it.

practice.question: For a two-sided test of mean abnormal return, what does H₀: μ = 0 mean?
practice.solution: It is the reference claim that the population mean abnormal return is zero percentage points for the defined population, window and design.

lessons.title: Compute and interpret a p-value
lessons.body:
A test statistic puts an estimate on a scale of standard errors from the null value. Suppose an illustrative sample estimates a mean abnormal return of 2.4 percentage points with standard error 1.2 percentage points. With μ₀ = 0, the statistic is t = (2.4 − 0) / 1.2 = 2.0. In a simple normal approximation, a two-sided p-value is about 0.0455. The correct reading is: if the null model and its assumptions were true, results at least this extreme would occur about 4.55% of the time. It is not P(H₀ true), not the probability the result happened by chance, and not a 95.45% probability of causality.

Suppose an illustrative employment programme is estimated to raise an employment rate by 2.4 percentage points, with a standard error of 1.2 percentage points. If the null model says the effect is zero, the estimate is 2.4 ÷ 1.2 = 2 standard errors from zero. A two-sided p-value is the probability, assuming that null model and the test’s assumptions, of getting a test statistic at least this far from zero in either direction; a value near 0.046 is one possible result. The steps are: state the null, calculate the estimate’s distance from it in standard-error units, then measure how much of the null reference distribution is at least as extreme.

That 0.046 is not a 4.6% chance that the programme has no effect, and it says nothing by itself about whether a 2.4-point change is worth the cost. The interpretation also depends on the design, model and analysis being reported. If researchers tried many outcomes or specifications and show only the smallest p-value, the single-test calculation hides the search. Report the estimate, units, interval, design and analysis choices together. The ASA statement and NIST interpretation guide linked below explain why a threshold such as 0.05 is not a verdict.

The tail calculation becomes clearer when the statistic is treated as a distance, not a score for truth. Illustrative synthetic example: an estimated change in a default rate is −1.5 percentage points, with a standard error of 0.75 percentage points, under a zero-change null. Then t = (−1.5 − 0) / 0.75 = −2.0; for a two-sided test, both tails count, so the p-value is approximately 0.046 under a normal reference distribution. This says that results at least 2 standard errors from zero would occur about 4.6% of the time if the model were correct. It does not establish a causal reduction or account for unreported analyses. For a fuller treatment, see ‘American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values’ in the linked sources.

Consider two illustrative, synthetic evaluations with the same standardized mean difference, 0.30 SD units, but different sample sizes. Under H₀: effect = 0 and a two-sided normal reference, with n = 100 the lab’s calculation is z = 0.30 × √100 = 0.30 × 10 = 3.00, giving p = 2[1 − Φ(3.00)] ≈ 0.0027. With n = 25, it is z = 0.30 × √25 = 0.30 × 5 = 1.50, giving p ≈ 0.1336. Thus the estimated magnitude is unchanged, while the larger sample makes the same signal more precisely measured and therefore less compatible with the null model. The p-value has not become an effect-size measure: 0.30 SD still requires a substantive interpretation in the outcome’s original units and context. This comparison assumes independent observations and a suitable normal approximation. If observations are clustered—such as workers within firms—the nominal n can overstate information; standard errors should reflect that dependence, or the displayed p-values can be too small. These values are synthetic demonstrations, not observed evidence or causal estimates.
lessons.takeaway: The p-value is a conditional tail probability under H₀, not a probability assigned to H₀ itself.

practice.question: Using the example, calculate t when the estimate is 2.4 percentage points, μ₀ is 0 and the standard error is 1.2 percentage points.
practice.hint: Subtract the null value, then divide by the standard error.
practice.solution: t = (2.4 − 0) / 1.2 = 2.0. The units cancel because both numerator and denominator are percentage points.

lessons.title: Read intervals and effect size together
lessons.body:
A p-value gives one aspect of evidence; an estimate and interval show magnitude and uncertainty. Continuing the illustrative example, 2.4 percentage points ± 1.96 × 1.2 percentage points gives an approximate 95% interval from 0.048 to 4.752 percentage points under the normal approximation. That interval is compatible with a small positive effect and with a much larger one, so practical importance remains a substantive question. Compare it with a pre-specified materiality threshold, such as 1 percentage point, and report units. A result can be statistically detectable but too small to matter after fees, risk or implementation costs; a meaningful effect can be imprecisely estimated.

Illustrative synthetic example — Suppose a randomly assigned job-search support programme is evaluated using participants’ annual earnings 12 months after enrolment. The estimated difference between the offered and comparison groups is £600 per worker per year, with a standard error of £250. Relative to a zero-effect null, the test statistic is 600 ÷ 250 = 2.4, giving an approximate two-sided normal p-value of 0.016. A rough 95% interval is £600 ± 1.96 × £250, or about £110 to £1,090 per worker per year. The estimate is positive and the interval excludes zero, but it spans effects below and above a pre-specified practical benchmark of £500 per year. Thus the data are fairly incompatible with zero under this model, while the programme’s economically meaningful size remains uncertain.

An interval and p-value can describe sampling evidence and precision; they cannot alone establish that the programme caused the earnings difference, that the effect lasts beyond 12 months, or that benefits exceed delivery costs. A key check is whether assignment was genuinely random and whether attrition, clustering by training centre, or unequal follow-up could change the standard error or comparison; compare results with reasonable design-appropriate analyses. Avoid saying that p = 0.016 means a 1.6% chance the null is true, or that the interval has a 95% probability of containing the fixed effect. The “American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values” and “NIST — Use and Interpretation of P-Values” in the linked sources below explain these cautions.

A useful habit is to compare an interval with a decision-relevant benchmark in the same units. Illustrative synthetic example: a policy estimate is an additional 18 minutes of weekly exercise per participant, with a standard error of 10 minutes. An approximate 95% interval is 18 ± 1.96 × 10 = 18 ± 19.6 minutes, or about −1.6 to 37.6 minutes per week. The estimate is positive, but the interval includes almost no change and effects above half an hour. If the practical benchmark is 30 minutes per week, the interval crosses it, so the study does not pin down whether that target is reached. This evidence alone does not prove the policy caused exercise changes or that benefits exceed costs. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 7: Inference for Numerical Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example — Suppose an estimated price elasticity of demand is −0.40, with standard error 0.15. A normal-approximation 95% interval is −0.40 ± 1.96 × 0.15 = [−0.694, −0.106]. If a firm raises price by 5%, the local constant-elasticity approximation predicts quantity falling by 0.40 × 5% = 2.0%; the interval implies a fall between 0.106 × 5% = 0.53% and 0.694 × 5% = 3.47%. With synthetic baseline sales of 100,000 units per month at £20 each (£2,000,000 monthly revenue), the point prediction gives revenue of £20 × 1.05 × 100,000 × 0.98 = £2,058,000, a £58,000 increase. Using the interval endpoints, revenue ranges from £2,000,000 × 1.05 × 0.9653 = £2,027,130 to £2,000,000 × 1.05 × 0.9947 = £2,088,870 per month. This translation shows why a statistically informative elasticity still requires a demand-model assumption, stable customer mix, no competitor response, and a check that a 5% change is local enough; the interval does not guarantee realized revenue.
lessons.takeaway: Report direction, magnitude, interval width and practical thresholds—not only a significance label.

practice.question: Does the illustrative interval [0.048, 4.752] percentage points prove the effect is economically important?
practice.hint: Compare the interval with a meaningful threshold and consider costs.
practice.solution: No. It indicates uncertainty about a positive mean under the stated model, but importance requires a domain threshold, costs, risk and context.

lessons.title: Why 0.05 is not a cliff
lessons.body:
The ASA advises against treating statistical significance as a binary discovery switch. A p-value of 0.049 and one of 0.051 provide closely related evidence, not opposite truths. The cutoff α = 0.05 is a planning convention that, for a specified procedure, controls the long-run Type I error rate when H₀ is true; it does not measure effect size or truth. “Fail to reject” is not proof of no effect. A small p-value can reflect a tiny effect in a huge sample, while a practically important effect can have a wide interval in a small or noisy sample. Explain uncertainty continuously and avoid cliff language.

Treat nearby p-values as a graded evidential difference, then inspect magnitude and precision. Illustrative synthetic example: Study A estimates a wage gain of $0.20 per hour with p = 0.049; Study B estimates $0.21 per hour with p = 0.051. The estimates differ by only $0.01 per hour, and rounding or modest model changes could affect the displayed p-values. Calling A “real” and B “no effect” creates a discontinuity unsupported by those numbers. The dollar amounts are not automatically useful: over 160 work hours, $0.20 per hour corresponds to $0.20 × 160 = $32 per month before taxes, assuming that schedule. Neither p-value proves causality, and neither assesses the worker’s costs or long-run consequences. For a fuller treatment, see ‘Wasserstein, Schirm & Lazar (2019) — Moving to a World Beyond p < 0.05’ in the linked sources.

Use the lab’s standardized-effect control to see why precision, not just magnitude, moves a p-value. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a productivity assessment has a standard deviation of 20 points and an estimated difference of 0.30 SD, equivalent to 0.30 × 20 = 6 points. With n = 100 independent observations under the lab’s normal approximation, the null-model statistic is z = 0.30 × √100 = 3.00; a two-sided p-value is approximately 2[1 − Φ(3.00)] = 0.0027. Keeping the same estimated 6-point difference but using n = 25 gives z = 0.30 × √25 = 1.50 and p ≈ 0.1336. The estimate and its practical interpretation did not change; the smaller sample made random uncertainty larger. These calculations assume the standardized statistic is appropriate and observations provide the stated information; dependence, non-normality, or a biased comparison can invalidate the approximation. Even the smaller p-value would describe incompatibility with a zero-effect model, not proof that a program caused the productivity difference or that six points is economically worthwhile.
lessons.takeaway: Use thresholds for decisions only in context; do not turn 0.05 into a universal truth boundary.

practice.question: What can a p-value above 0.05 mean besides “there is no effect”?
practice.solution: The estimate may be imprecise, the sample may be small, noise may be high, or the design may be weak. Non-rejection is not proof that the effect is exactly zero.

lessons.title: Power, errors and study design
lessons.body:
Before collecting data, specify a practically meaningful effect, expected variability, sample size, α and the test direction. Type I error means rejecting a true H₀; Type II error means failing to reject a false H₀. Power is 1 − β, the probability of detecting a chosen alternative under the design. Larger samples, lower noise, larger effects and better measurements generally increase power, but power is not a guarantee for one study. A low-powered study may miss a meaningful effect, while a very large study can detect a negligible one. Design quality and measurement validity matter before arithmetic. A credible power calculation should also reflect attrition, clustering or repeated observations when those features are expected.

Power is easiest to communicate with a target effect and a probability scale. Illustrative synthetic example: before a survey, researchers define a meaningful improvement of 4 percentage points in the share completing training and plan a design with β = 0.20. Power = 1 − β = 1 − 0.20 = 0.80, or 80%, for detecting that specified 4-point improvement under the planned assumptions. It does not mean an 80% chance that the eventual estimate is correct. If only 60% of sampled people respond, the effective sample may be smaller and power may fall; nonresponse can also introduce bias that more observations do not automatically fix. The 4 percentage points describe a difference in rates, not a 4% relative increase. For a fuller treatment, see ‘OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 6: Inference for Categorical Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic planning example: suppose an economist wants to detect a standardized training effect of d = 0.50 SD with two equal-sized randomized groups, using a two-sided α = 0.05 test and 80% power. Under a normal approximation, the required number per arm is n = 2(z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈₀)²/d² = 2(1.96 + 0.842)²/0.50² = 62.8, so round up to 63 participants per arm (126 analyzed participants). If the analyst anticipates 20% attrition, enrollment should be ceil(63/0.80) = 79 per arm, or 158 total; rounding up matters because fractional people cannot be enrolled. This calculation treats the SD as known, assumes independent observations, equal allocation, a correctly specified outcome, and a normal approximation. Clustering, unequal variances, noncompliance, or a smaller true effect would require a larger or richer calculation. The p-value lab can show how a standardized effect and n change a two-sided tail area, but that tail area is not itself a guarantee that the planned study will achieve 80% power.
lessons.takeaway: Power concerns a specified effect and design; it is not the probability that a finding is true.
lessons.formula: power = 1 − β; α = long-run Type I error rate under H₀

practice.question: If β = 0.20 for a specified effect and design, what is the power?
practice.solution: Power = 1 − 0.20 = 0.80, or 80%. This is conditional on the chosen effect, model, sample size and assumptions.

lessons.title: Multiplicity and the search process
lessons.body:
Testing many outcomes, firms, subgroups, event windows or model specifications changes the chance of a small p-value. Even if each test uses α = 0.05, a collection of tests can produce at least one apparently unusual result by chance. Optional stopping, trying alternatives and reporting only favorable results can make nominal error rates misleading. Pre-register primary outcomes, hypotheses, stopping rules and analysis choices when feasible. Disclose all tested analyses, distinguish confirmatory from exploratory work, and use a multiplicity method when the question requires control of family-wise error or false-discovery rate. Transparency lets readers judge how much search occurred before the headline result was selected.

Multiplicity can be shown with a simple probability calculation. Illustrative synthetic example: imagine 20 independent tests, each using a 5% cutoff, while every null hypothesis is actually true. The probability of no false positive is approximately 0.95^20 ≈ 0.358, so the probability of at least one false positive is 1 − 0.358 = 0.642, or about 64.2%. Independence is a simplifying assumption, and dependence can change the number, but searching still matters. If an analyst examines 20 monthly event windows and highlights the one with p = 0.04, that p-value describes the selected window’s calculation, not the whole search process. Disclosure, preregistration, or an appropriate adjustment is needed; the arithmetic does not prove every finding is false. For a fuller treatment, see ‘American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values’ in the linked sources.

A practical way to act on a disclosed search is the Holm step-down procedure. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose four pre-specified null hypotheses concern four different outcomes, and their valid two-sided p-values are 0.003, 0.018, 0.041 and 0.20. First sort them from smallest to largest, then compare the jth value with α/(m−j+1), using α = 0.05 and m = 4. The thresholds are 0.0125, 0.0167, 0.0250 and 0.0500: 0.003 passes the first comparison, but 0.018 exceeds 0.0167, so the step-down sequence stops and only the first hypothesis is rejected. This controls the family-wise error rate at 5% under the procedure’s assumptions, rather than pretending that four unadjusted 5% tests form one 5% decision rule. The calculation does not establish that the first outcome is economically important or causal: report its effect estimate, uncertainty, outcome units, design, and whether the family was defined before looking at results. If the outcomes were selected after seeing the data, adjustment alone cannot recreate preregistration or remove selection bias.
lessons.takeaway: A p-value is only as honest as the analysis search that produced it.

practice.question: Why should an event study disclose that 20 windows were examined before one p-value was reported?
practice.solution: Searching many windows increases the chance of finding a small p-value by chance. Disclosure supports appropriate interpretation and possible multiplicity adjustment.

lessons.title: Association, prediction and causality
lessons.body:
A p-value can quantify incompatibility with a null model for an association, but it cannot identify a causal mechanism by itself. Prediction asks how well an outcome can be anticipated for new cases; causality asks what would change under an intervention. Confounding, reverse causality, selection and time trends can create associations in financial data. Random assignment can support causal comparison for the assigned population; observational regression needs explicit identification assumptions. Report the target population, data-generating process, timing, missingness and robustness checks. A statistically detectable relationship may predict poorly out of sample, and a predictive relationship need not be causal or actionable.

Separate the unit of prediction from the unit of causal change. Illustrative synthetic example: across 100 synthetic firms, an observational regression finds that each additional 1 percentage point of quarterly sales growth is associated with 0.3 percentage points higher quarterly return. The arithmetic says a 2-point sales-growth difference corresponds to 0.3 × 2 = 0.6 percentage points of fitted return difference, not that changing sales growth would cause a 0.6-point return. Industry conditions could influence both variables, and an average association may predict poorly for a new firm. A causal claim would need a design or assumptions addressing confounding, timing and selection. The units are percentage points of return, not percent probability and not a guaranteed dollar gain. For a fuller treatment, see ‘NIST — Use and Interpretation of P-Values’ in the linked sources.

A useful prediction check is to freeze the model before looking at future outcomes. Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a researcher uses eight earlier firms to fit next-quarter return from sales growth, then evaluates four later firms. The four model errors (predicted minus realized return) are 0.4, −0.6, 0.8 and −0.2 percentage points, so the test-set mean squared error is (0.4² + (−0.6)² + 0.8² + (−0.2)²)/4 = 1.20/4 = 0.30 pp², and RMSE is √0.30 = 0.55 pp. A simple benchmark that predicts the training-period mean has errors 0.7, −1.1, 1.0 and −0.9 pp: MSE = 3.51/4 = 0.8775 pp² and RMSE ≈ 0.94 pp. The model therefore improves this small synthetic test by about 0.39 pp of RMSE, a predictive result—not evidence that sales growth causes returns. A time-ordered split avoids using future information; repeated periods are needed to assess stability, and trading costs or decision thresholds determine whether a 0.39 pp improvement is economically useful.
lessons.takeaway: Statistical evidence, prediction and causal claims answer different questions and require different support.

practice.question: Does p = 0.03 for an event-study coefficient prove the disclosure caused the return?
practice.solution: No. It is evidence against the specified null under the event-study assumptions. Causality requires a credible design and assumptions that address confounding and timing.

lessons.title: Beyond statistical significance: transparent conclusions
lessons.body:
A responsible conclusion combines the estimate, units, interval, p-value, design, assumptions, analysis search and practical threshold. State what was planned, what was exploratory, which outcomes were missing and whether results are robust to reasonable alternatives. The ASA principles emphasize that scientific conclusions should not depend only on crossing a threshold, that p-values do not measure the probability a hypothesis is true, and that context and transparency matter. Connect evidence to uncertainty and decision consequences without presenting a financial recommendation. “Beyond Statistical Significance” is a useful theme here: the goal is richer reasoning, not replacing one ritual with another. Readers should be able to audit the path from question to conclusion.

A transparent conclusion can be written as a compact audit trail. Illustrative synthetic example: a randomized pilot estimates a reduction of 6 percentage points in missed appointments, with a 95% interval from −11 to −1 percentage points and p = 0.02. Report the outcome unit, follow-up period, assignment rule, missing-data handling and whether this was the pre-specified primary outcome. The interval suggests reductions from 1 to 11 percentage points are compatible with the analysis, while the sign convention must be stated clearly. It does not show that savings exceed programme costs, that the effect persists after six months, or that the result generalizes to other clinics. A reader should also see exploratory outcomes and deviations from plan, rather than only the favorable headline. For a fuller treatment, see ‘American Statistical Association — Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values’ in the linked sources.

Illustrative synthetic example: suppose a pre-specified evaluation estimates a standardized outcome difference from n = 25 independent units, with the outcome expressed in standard-deviation units. Assume the simple normal approximation used by the lab is reasonable under a null of zero difference. First compute the standard error as 1/√25 = 0.20 SD; then z = 0.30/0.20 = 1.50. A two-sided null tail is approximately p = 2[1 − Φ(1.50)] = 0.134, so this sample does not make the estimate unusual at α = 0.05. The approximate 95% interval is 0.30 ± 1.96(0.20) = [−0.092, 0.692] SD. That range includes a small negative effect, no effect, and a potentially meaningful positive effect; it therefore signals imprecision, not proof of no difference. Before changing policy, report the estimand, unit of analysis, missing outcomes, and whether the normal/independence assumptions hold. If assignment was observational, this uncertainty calculation still describes an association under the model, not a causal effect.
lessons.takeaway: Transparent, effect-focused reporting is more informative than a binary p < 0.05 claim.
lessons.formula: Evidence report = estimate + interval + p-value + design + assumptions + practical context

caseStudy: Consider an illustrative event study of a new disclosure format and a diversified firm's 3-day abnormal return. The analyst pre-specifies H₀: μ = 0 percentage points, a two-sided alternative, a market-adjustment model, a 3-day window and a materiality threshold of 1 percentage point. The sample estimate is 2.4 percentage points with a standard error of 1.2, giving t = 2.0 and an approximate two-sided p-value of 0.0455; the approximate 95% interval is [0.048, 4.752] percentage points. This is not a 95.45% probability that the disclosure caused the return. The interval spans effects below and above the practical threshold, so economic importance remains uncertain. The analyst should disclose whether other windows, firms, outcomes or specifications were tried, account for multiplicity where appropriate, and report missing events and robustness checks. Without randomization or a credible identification strategy, the result is an association under a model, not proof of causality. The numbers are simulated for teaching, not a historical dataset, forecast or investment advice.
misconceptions: p = 0.03 means a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true, or a 97% chance the alternative is true. The p-value is calculated conditional on the null model and assumptions.

p < 0.05 proves an important, useful or causal effect, while p > 0.05 proves no effect. Thresholds do not measure magnitude, practical importance or identification, and non-rejection may reflect low power.
A large sample or narrow interval fixes bias. More observations can reduce random uncertainty but cannot repair selection, confounding, bad measurement or a misspecified design.
Trying many outcomes, windows or specifications leaves the false-positive risk unchanged. Multiplicity, selective reporting and optional stopping can make nominal error rates misleading.
A statistically significant association is automatically a good prediction or investment opportunity. Association, prediction, causality and decision usefulness are distinct claims.

quiz.question: Which is the most accurate plain-English description of p = 0.03 under a specified null model?
options: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true.
If the null model and assumptions were true, results this extreme or more would occur about 3% of the time.
There is a 97% chance the alternative is true.
quiz.explanation: That is the conditional definition. It does not give the probability that either hypothesis is true, the probability of causality, or the practical importance of the effect.
